title: A Conservator on Tape
passage:
The certificate came in wrapped in a tea towel, torn across in about 1974 and mended at home with a strip of clear tape. Three flakes of film clung along one edge; the rest was a hard brown band the width of the strip.

“People ask me to take the tape off,” says Odette Fenniscarth, a paper conservator. “Mostly there’s no tape left; the film let go years ago. What’s left is the glue.” She turns the certificate to the light. “The rubber in it has oxidised – that’s the brown – and the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper. Where the glue went in, the sheet’s gone like greased paper; you can read the back through it.”

“Tape holds a tear for ten years and marks the sheet for a hundred,” she says. She warms a mend from last year, and the film lifts and brings most of the glue with it. On a mend as old as this one, heat does nothing. The glue has gone hard, she says, so only a solvent will move it, and which solvent depends on what the glue was made of. About the stain itself she is careful: “The brown that’s in the fibres I can lighten. I don’t promise to take it out.”

– Oscar Goddard

questions.rationale: Option C is the key. It paraphrases the conservator’s own account of what the adhesive does to the sheet: “the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper. Where the glue went in, the sheet’s gone like greased paper; you can read the back through it.” Greased paper lets light through, and being able to read the back of a sheet through the stained area is what translucent means, so C restates the passage’s mechanism in different words. Option A tempts because it reuses two things the passage really says – that the rubber in the glue has oxidised and that the film came away – and reassigns them: it makes the plasticiser the thing that has turned brown. The passage says the opposite in one sentence: “The rubber in it has oxidised – that’s the brown – and the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper.” The brown is the oxidised rubber; the plasticiser is the part that went into the sheet. A reader who has not sorted the two components will find A natural, which is why it has to be checked against that sentence. Option B swaps her two methods. She warms a mend from last year so that the film lifts and takes most of the glue with it, and she turns to a solvent once the glue has gone hard; on a mend as old as this one, “heat does nothing”. B gives heat to the hardened glue and solvent to the soft, which is the reverse pairing. The everyday experience that warmth softens hard things makes the swap sound right, and only the passage says which way round the two methods actually go. Option D overshoots what she promises. Matching the solvent to the glue is in the passage (“which solvent depends on what the glue was made of”), but the outcome D attaches to it is not. What she says about the brown already in the fibres sets a limit rather than a promise: “The brown that’s in the fibres I can lighten. I don’t promise to take it out.” D turns a limited result into a complete one. None of A, B or D is true as written, so the question does not turn on a best fit; each fails against a sentence a careful reader can point to.
